cse-2006-cs-67.approach: Test each query on the tie case and on the top customer. Query1 counts ties (including A itself) so tied customers get a rank too large; Query2 uses an inner join, so the customer(s) with the largest balance produce no row at all.

steps.title: Query1 on a tie
steps.body:
Query1 rank $=\#\{B : B.balance \ge A.balance\}$, which counts $A$ itself and every customer tied with $A$.

Two customers both with the largest balance: each gets $\text{count}=2$, i.e. rank 2, but the specification says rank 1. So Query1 is **wrong** (it is right only when there are no ties).

steps.title: Query2 on the top customer
steps.body: Query2 rank $=1+\#\{B : B.balance > A.balance\}$ — the right formula. But the `where` filter runs before `group by`: for a customer with the largest balance no pair $(A,B)$ satisfies $A.balance < B.balance$, so that customer forms **no group and gets no row**. Query2 is therefore also **wrong** (top-ranked customers vanish).

steps.body: Empty `account`: both queries return the empty set — identical. One customer $c$: Query1 gives $(c,1)$, Query2 gives nothing — different. So statement 1 is true and statement 4 is true; 2 and 3 are false.

steps.title: Statement 5
steps.body:
The relational version is a self-join: $\Theta(n^2)$ pairs. Sorting/scanning in decreasing balance order and assigning ranks costs $O(n\log n)$. So 5 is false.

Correct pair: **1 and 4**.

steps.body: If $P_3$ has not yet passed line 4, it now sees $4\ne3$ and spins forever.
